extracted.intended_audience: small and medium business owners, PR professionals, communications staff, and entrepreneurs who must write and distribute press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guide to writing, formatting, and distributing press releases that journalists will read and use; covers element-by-element composition, headline and body guidance, distribution channels, and audience targeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable press release length
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptable length of a news release is 300 to 500 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be succinct because journalists read hundreds of releases a day; longer is not better. Keep content focused and avoid filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard elements and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Years of tradition have established a standard set of elements for a press release, each of which should be in a certain order and formatted in a certain way. Journalists expect this information, in this order and format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include (in order): Headline, Dateline, Opening Paragraph (lead), Body Paragraphs, Boilerplate, Contact Information. Deviating from expected order reduces effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline length and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release headline tells journalists the purpose of the press release in a one-line statement that’s 60 to 80 characters in length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it attention-grabbing while truthful and relevant. It’s the single most important element—if it’s dull, journalists will pass. Use a concise summary of the news and primary benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline tone and style
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline should grab the reader’s attention while remaining truthful and relevant to your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ALL CAPS (hard to read), sensationalist jargon, fluff words like 'Fantastic' or 'Life-Changing', and industry-specific jargon. Use title case. Consider an optional subhead in sentence case to elaborate without overshadowing the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Datelines appear in the first line of press releases and should be formatted as CITY, State, Month Day, Year (distribution tag, e.g., (PRNewswire)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The city and state should be the location of the company/organization; the date should reflect when the release is sent. The distribution method tag is usually added by the newswire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead sentence / Opening paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening sentence (lead) succinctly summarizes what is being announced while hooking the audience into your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the full release first, then craft the opening paragraph as an executive-summary-style hook. Ensure it contains the most important facts and entices the reader to continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body structure and length
rubrics_metrics.description: The body section usually consists of three to five paragraphs (guidance says three to six paragraphs) that give more details about the announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill the body only with content that relates directly to the opening/headline. Arrange paragraphs to expand on the 5Ws and supporting details; do not include irrelevant material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the 5Ws
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the essential 5Ws of content: Who? What? Where? When? Why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each W is addressed. Journalists scan for these facts—present them clearly and early. Use paragraph arrangement to make these elements easy to find.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relevant, concise quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: A quote from you or a company exec does more than add significance; it positions you as an authority and makes future coverage more likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make quotes relevant to the news and avoid generic promotional language. Use subject-matter experts or executives to reinforce credibility. Keep quotes short and attributable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate placement and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The boilerplate is a short paragraph near the end that explains the identity of your company/organization and what it does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boilerplates are optional but useful; keep them brief and reusable across releases. Place them right before contact information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact information specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Include contact information: name, title, phone, email, full website URL, and company name. This should not be the general company info but a specific individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct journalists to a specific person who will respond. Ensure the listed contact actually answers calls/emails and reach that person directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-release marker
rubrics_metrics.description: Finished? End your press release with three pound signs (###).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the commonly accepted signifier of the end of the release and should be used to indicate there is no more content.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP Style adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard for press release writing is the AP Stylebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AP style as journalists’ preferred style; you don’t need to memorize it but having a copy helps. Editors may be lenient, but AP remains the go-to style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release should have news value to the audience of the journalist who receives the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and demonstrate the newsworthy angle—why this matters to the journalist’s readership. Convert business developments into news hooks rather than advertising copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid advertising language and fluff
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut the fluff, lose the sensationalism. Words like 'Fantastic,' 'Great,' 'Wonderful,' 'Life-Changing,' and heavy editorial 'bling' do not belong in headlines or releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fact-based, concise language. Releases that read like ads are ignored by reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting journalists and building relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Research target journalists who cover stories about your company’s causes and products; develop long-term relationships with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit releases directly to journalists who cover the relevant beat when you have a relationship. Regular submissions build familiarity—small businesses should consider monthly releases; respond quickly when journalists contact you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution channels and newswire tiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Most companies and publicists rely on a newswire to distribute press releases; top newswires include PR Newswire and Business Wire (Tier 1) and GlobeNewswire (Tier 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the right newswire and categories for your content. Be aware of costs (e.g., ~$1200 for Tier 1 for a 500-word release) and that newswires add distribution tags and enforce submission standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newswire submission standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When sending press releases to newswires, writers must follow the newswire’s submission standards that guard against defamation, nudity, and advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review and comply with the chosen newswire’s rules to avoid rejection. Avoid content that could be construed as defamatory or overt advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release types and appropriate use
rubrics_metrics.description: Common types of media releases include the standard release, the media advisory, and the embargoed release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a standard release for milestone announcements, a media advisory to inform about upcoming press conferences, and embargoed releases to provide time-sensitive data intended for publication at a specific date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event press release best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing an event press release requires giving journalists facts about the event that are exciting enough to share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include purpose, setting, desired attendees, 5Ws, and proofread dates/addresses to avoid credibility loss. Target journalists who cover events relevant to your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product press release best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: For product releases, craft an exciting headline that introduces the product, shows uniqueness, and highlights its primary benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide features in the opening paragraph, supply supporting data/statistics in the body, include quotes and backstory, and provide contact info for technical specs (because full specs rarely fit a short release). Avoid blatant sales copy; support claims with data and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of data, statistics, and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use data and statistics to support claimed benefits; journalists may fact-check and ask for sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include credible data and be prepared to provide sources. Fact-based releases lend more credibility than those with promotional language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading and factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreading event press releases is crucial; grammatically correct releases are easier to read and incorrect dates/addresses lower credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully proofread for grammar, dates, locations, contact details, and factual accuracy before distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Template and formatting availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a press release template (Word or Google Docs) to make formatting easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following a standard template helps ensure you include required elements and adhere to expected order and format preferred by journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution etiquette — don’t spam editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t tarnish your good name spamming editors!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target releases, avoid mass irrelevant blasts, and maintain professionalism in frequency and content. Over-mailing harms relationships and credibility.
